newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel-PLO summit set for midnight at border.
newsitem.headline: Israel-PLO summit set for midnight at border.

text.p: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat scheduled a meeting for late on Tuesday to try to break a deadlock over extending Palestinian rule to the West Bank town of Hebron.
U.S. and Palestinian officials said Netanyahu and Arafat, chairman of the PLO, would meet at midnight (2200 GMT) at the Erez crossing linking Israel to the self-ruled Gaza Strip.
Their negotiators would meet at a Jerusalem hotel starting at 6 p.m. (1600 GMT) after Ross reports to Netanyahu on the progress of the talks at 5.30 p.m. (1530 GMT), officials said.
"The negotiators will meet at 6 o'clock in Jerusalem to try to resolve the issues that will pave the way for the summit at midnight," Arafat's adviser Nabil Abu Rdainah told Reuters.
"If all the issues are not resolved by the negotiators, the summit will be a working meeting. Therefore the agreement is possible tonight or tomorrow," he said.
"We have been working and there will be a meeting tonight between the prime minister and the chairman at Erez. It'll be a late-night meeting," U.S. envoy Dennis Ross told Israel Radio.
An adviser to Arafat said earlier the Palestinian leader was ready to meet Netanyahu to remove obstacles holding up a Hebron deal. PLO officials said talks were snagged on four issues.

Hebron, a West Bank flashpoint, is home to 400 militant Jewish settlers and 100,000 Arabs. It was to be handed over to the Palestinians last March but violence, security concerns and Israel's change of government in June delayed the pullback.
It is the last of seven Palestinian cities that were to be turned over to Palestinian self-rule under a 1995 interim peace accord signed by the previous Israeli government.

While Israel's talks with Palestinians have been slow, there have been no peace talks with Syria. Zeev Maoz, head of Tel Aviv University's Jaffee Centre for Strategic Studies, warned on Tuesday of a rising prospect of war with Syria.
"In my assessment, as long as the political stalemate continues, the probability of war rises in a very significant way," he said.
Arafat's adviser Nabil Abu Rdainah told Reuters: "The remaining issues (on Hebron) are very silly. They could be overcome very quickly."
Netanyahu's spokesman Shai Bazak would not discuss remaining difficulties, but PLO officials charged the talks were stuck on:
- Israel's demand the Palestinian Authority extradite to Israel Arabs wanted by the Jewish state.
- Israel's demand for a veto over the names of all PLO police set to serve in Hebron.
- Israel's insistence the PLO promise to crack down on militant groups.
- A dispute over Palestinian control of Hebron's al-Ibrahimi mosque, part of a shrine holy to Moslems and Jews as the burial place of the biblical Abraham.
Israeli and Palestine Liberation Organisation peace teams ended late-night talks early on Tuesday after a bomb scare forced them to change venue.
"We have reached our point of maximum flexibility," Israeli Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai said. "The Palestinians need to come and sign the agreement and move the process forward."

Progress in the U.S.-brokered talks after months of impasse came during mediation by Jordan's King Hussein on Sunday. The king nudged the sides toward a compromise timetable for three further Israeli withdrawals from rural West Bank areas now due to be completed by mid-1998.
